title: Major corruption scandals shake Ukraine. What do Brussels and experts say about its efforts to clean up?
content:
Corruption is one of the main issues exploited by Russian propaganda to undermine Western support for Ukraine. Over the past year, narratives claiming that all Western aid donated to Kyiv is bound to be stolen have been reinforced by several major corruption scandals, some of which reach into the closest circles of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.

The biggest corruption scandal to rock Ukraine’s political scene during this period was the Midas case in the energy sector. It cost two ministers their positions, as well as Andriy Yermak, the president’s right-hand man.

There was also significant attention surrounding investigations into several former officials from the presidential office, including Yermak, over suspicions of money laundering and the embezzlement of millions.

Another major scandal was uncovered by anti-corruption authorities in recent days. During an operation codenamed Carthage, they revealed allegations that senior officers of Ukraine’s security service, the SBU, had protected fraudulent call centres and other criminal organisations, including the Chimprom drug cartel.

title: ‘A fascist salute on the euro’: Kremlin narrative about Baltic coins backing Ukraine resurfaces in Slovakia and Czechia
content:
Every year, each euro area member state may issue two commemorative two-euro coins with a design of its own. Most countries use them to mark themes of major national or European importance.

The Baltic states used this option to show their support for Ukraine. In 2022, following the start of the war in Ukraine, Estonia issued a coin bearing the inscription ‘Glory to Ukraine’. A year later, the other two Baltic states followed: Latvia with a coin carrying the same slogan and Lithuania with the slogan ‘Together with Ukraine’. Like all other commemorative two-euro coins, they are legal tender throughout the euro area, including Slovakia.

Although they have been in circulation for years, the coins repeatedly resurfaced as a topic in 2026. In Slovakia, they were brought up in October by Ľuboš Blaha, a Member of the European Parliament for Prime Minister Robert Fico’s Smer party, who sits with the non-attached members. According to him, the slogan ‘Glory to Ukraine’ refers mainly to the historical controversies of Ukrainian nationalism and to the tragic events of the Volhynia massacre during the Second World War.

title: Hungarian government moves ahead of EU directive with its own women’s rights reform package
content:
• Hungary’s new Tisza government has unveiled a comprehensive women’s rights reform package, marking a significant departure from the policies of previous Orbán governments, under which women’s rights advocates say legal protections steadily deteriorated.
  • Hungary plans to ratify the Istanbul Convention and strengthen legislation against domestic and sexual violence, leaving only four EU member states — Bulgaria, Czechia, Lithuania and Slovakia — that have not ratified the treaty.
  • The government intends to remove prescription requirements for emergency contraception, making the morning-after pill more accessible, although its relatively high cost will remain a significant obstacle for many women.
  • Hungary will ease its controversial fetal heartbeat decree, allowing women seeking an abortion to choose whether to listen to the fetal heartbeat rather than making it mandatory, but critics warn that the revised rules could still expose women to pressure from doctors.

title: Spain’s open-door migration model: A European alternative or a strategic dilemma?
content:
During the opening ceremony of the 30th Ibero-American Summit, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez argued that shared culture and values should translate into stronger political, economic and diplomatic influence. Against a global backdrop of increasingly isolationist tendencies, he called for a different approach: greater openness, cooperation and international engagement.

In his speech, he described Madrid as one of the hearts where [missing ending in source material] beats.

Sánchez recalled that the first meeting of Latin American countries took place in Guadalajara 35 years ago. It marked the culmination of decades of exchanges, connections and dialogue between the two sides of the Atlantic. He highlighted the cultural and linguistic similarities that unite more than 700 million Spanish- and Portuguese-speaking people. He also included indigenous languages in this shared heritage, emphasising the geopolitical significance of a common cultural community.

He cited Frida Kahlo, Pablo Picasso, Oscar Niemeyer and Antoni Gaudí, alongside Gabriel García Márquez, José Saramago and Rosalía, as examples of this shared cultural heritage.

title: Far-right extremist or Ukrainian Fighter? Disinformation rewrote the story of the Krakow attack
content:
Saturday’s events in Krakow triggered a wave of disinformation across the internet. Within hours, false claims began circulating about both the attacker and the circumstances surrounding the shooting.

The perpetrator was attributed radically different political views, linked to Ukrainian military formations, and featured in manipulated photographs and videos generated using artificial intelligence.

There were also false reports concerning the response of emergency services and the alleged absence of police officers at the scene. The misleading claims came from anonymous social media accounts as well as statements made in traditional media outlets.

The incident has also demonstrated how powerful and convincing artificial intelligence has become as a tool for spreading disinformation. AI-generated content is increasingly sophisticated, and in many cases it is difficult to determine whether an image or video is genuine without using specialised tools to analyse it.

title: Trump loses Congress, but Europe may not benefit
content:
Republicans have experienced a night they are unlikely to forget. Their opponents, the Democratic Party, won control of both chambers of the US Congress in midterm elections (3 November). As a result, Trump will now face a stronger political counterweight in both the House of Representatives and the Senate.

His symbolic defeat is being celebrated not only in the United States but also in Europe. According to a recent pan-European poll, 58 percent of Europeans supported a Democratic victory in the elections, compared with just 18 percent who favoured the Republicans.

Waking up to a “blue morning” may have given pro-democratic voices across the EU a boost. In practical terms, however, not all that much is changing for Brussels.

The Democrats’ victory is likely to make governing at home considerably more difficult for Trump. It could lead to more intensive investigations into his administration, tougher budget negotiations and the blocking of his nominees. However, it may do little to fundamentally change his conduct on the international stage.

title: Poland’s new security reality: When terrorism hits close to home
content:
Until recently, terrorism was far less common in Poland than in countries such as France, Belgium or Spain. Attacks involving firearms were virtually unheard of. The main security concerns identified by the police included sabotage, disinformation, cyberattacks and espionage. These threats were largely linked to Poland’s geographical proximity to Russia, which continues its war against Ukraine while conducting hybrid operations against NATO and EU member states.

The events of 7 November 2026 have shifted these priorities. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk described the incident as an act of terrorism. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said the evidence collected so far suggested that the perpetrator was fascinated by far-right ideology. However, the authorities have not confirmed any links to radical organisations, nor has any foreign involvement been established.

Above all, the incident highlighted how difficult it can be to prevent an attack in the heart of a major city.

Dr Paulina Piasecka, director of the Terrorism Research Centre at Collegium Civitas, believes the response of Kraków’s emergency services demonstrated the readiness of Poland’s state institutions.

title: Good neighbours, complicated history: What Poles and Germans really think
content:
Thirty-five years after signing their Treaty on Good Neighbourship, Poland and Germany remain closely connected. But how do people on both sides of the border actually view their relationship? And do they see each other as equal partners?

These are some of the questions explored in the latest edition of the Polish-German Barometer, titled Between Cooperation and Security: 35 Years After the Treaty on Good Neighbourship.

One of the biggest differences between Polish and German respondents concerns how Germany has addressed its crimes and acknowledged the suffering inflicted on Poland during World War II.

As many as 44% of Germans believe their country has already done enough in this regard. In Poland, only 18% share that view.

The issue is even more prominent among respondents who have a negative opinion of Polish-German relations: 61% of them point to the failure to fully address German wartime crimes as a key reason.

Germans, meanwhile, tend to blame poor relations on political differences (43%) and the policies of Polish governments towards Berlin (38%). Historical issues rank only third.

title: EU steps up Black Sea security as Russian threats mount
content:
European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen’s visit has placed Romania and Bulgaria at the centre of the EU’s response to the deepening security crisis in the Black Sea. Its most significant outcome is the acceleration of work on a joint maritime security hub – a project that will test whether Europe can turn its strategic commitments into genuine operational capabilities.

The Black Sea is no longer merely a regional theatre of conflict. It is becoming a test for NATO and the EU: can they protect commercial shipping, energy infrastructure and the territory of member states without triggering a wider confrontation? In October alone, at least 10 merchant vessels were attacked near the Romanian and Bulgarian coasts or within those countries’ territorial waters. Four vessels sank, while 34 seafarers were reported dead or missing.

title: Europe seeks talks with Russia, but who will decide the terms of peace?
content:
• Europe selects its representatives for peace talks – The E5 countries and representatives of European Union institutions are expected to take part in the negotiations.
  • Kallas warns against concessions to Moscow – Russia is making maximalist demands, while Europe must maintain a united position.
  • Divisions within the European Union remain apparent – Member states still need to agree on a common negotiating mandate and the conditions for ending the war.
  • Pressure on Russia is set to continue – The European Union is preparing further sanctions and measures targeting Russia’s ability to finance its war.
